813.title: The cathedral labyrinth
813.hook: at Chartres, pilgrims walk a winding path to the center as a prayer
813.carry: the long way is the way
813.howItsDone: Some churches and retreat centers have labyrinths on the floor or the grounds, and people walk them slowly as a form of prayer or reflection, sometimes at set times when the path is cleared.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Hildegard's music, and your line, feather on the breath of God. A new week starts here.

Stand in the nave of Chartres Cathedral, in France, and look down. Set into the stone floor is a great circle: one winding path, dark lines curving around a flower-shaped center. When it's open for walking, people step onto it one after another and begin. No one is meant to race. No one is meant to cut across. The path swings toward the center, then away again, out toward the edge, then back, until it seems you'll never get there. And then you do.
screen: `A CIRCLE SET IN THE STONE FLOOR.`

segments.voice: First, a labyrinth isn't a maze. A maze is a puzzle, built to trick you, full of dead ends and wrong turns. A labyrinth has one path. You can't get lost in it; you only have to keep walking. On the Chartres floor the path brings you close to the center, then swings you all the way out to the edge, then back, again and again. The way in feels like the wrong way, and it isn't. It's the only way there is. How did medieval Christians use it? The floor itself doesn't say. Some readers suggest pilgrims walked it as a pilgrimage in miniature, a journey to Jerusalem on a cathedral floor. That's a story often told, and historians aren't certain of it. What's clear is how people use it now: slowly, as a prayer with the feet. Some walkers think of it as a journey with stages: going in, letting things go; resting at the center; coming out, carrying something back into the world. Scripture gives the walk its words. The letter to the Hebrews says the people of faith "confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth." A pilgrim is someone on the way, not yet home. And a psalm, in the King James words: "Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path." A lamp for the feet lights the next step, not the whole road. The labyrinth teaches the same thing in stone. You never need to see the center. You only need the next turn.
screen: `THE WAY IN FEELS LIKE THE WRONG WAY.`

segments.voice: If you can stand, walk a wide, slow circle that tightens toward a center point, pause there, then turn and unwind it back out, in small steps. If you pray, carry a name or a worry in, set it down at the center, and walk out without it. If you can't stand or walk right now, trace a spiral with one finger on your palm or a table, in and out, as slowly as you can.
Cathedral labyrinth. One winding path set in a church floor, walked slowly as a prayer, with no dead ends and no shortcuts.
Your line: the long way is the way. No dead ends, only turns. Until tomorrow.

814.title: Francis kisses the leper
814.hook: the rich young man who feared lepers dismounts and kisses one
814.howItsDone: Franciscan friars and sisters, and other Christians inspired by Francis, often serve people who are sick, poor or shunned, and Franciscans still read his Testament as a key to how his life changed.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the cathedral labyrinth, and your line, the long way is the way.

A young man is riding on the plain below Assisi. He's the son of a cloth merchant, used to money, fine clothes and good company. And there's one sight he can't bear: people with leprosy. By his own later account, even seeing them was bitter to him. Now, on the road ahead, there's a man with leprosy. Everything in the rider wants to look away and ride on. Instead, his early biographers say, he gets down from his horse. He gives the man money. And he kisses his hand.
screen: `A RICH YOUNG MAN ON A HORSE.`

segments.voice: The young man is Francis of Assisi. Near the end of his life, in the short text called his Testament, he looked back on this as where his new life began. In paraphrase: when I was in sin, it seemed too bitter to me to see lepers. And the Lord himself led me among them, and I showed mercy to them. And when I left them, what had seemed bitter to me was turned into sweetness of soul and body. Notice who leads in his telling. Not Francis: the Lord himself led me among them. And notice what changed. Not the people with leprosy; they were exactly who they had been. What changed was what tasted bitter and what tasted sweet, inside Francis. His biographers add that soon afterward he went to live among them, washing their sores and serving them, kissing hands he once couldn't look at. In Matthew's Gospel, a man with leprosy kneels and asks to be made clean, and Matthew writes, in the King James words: "Jesus put forth his hand, and touched him, saying, I will; be thou clean." He touched him. Before anything else happened, a hand reached out. Francis's kiss on the road echoes that reach. One word about words. The old word leper names a person by an illness. This lesson says people with leprosy where it can. The title keeps the old word because the old stories use it.
screen: `THE LORD HIMSELF LED ME AMONG THEM.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing or one person you steer around: a neighbor, a phone call, a part of town, a conversation. Without forcing anything, picture yourself getting down from the horse, stopping, then stepping a little closer, and notice what happens in you as you come nearer. If you pray, ask to be led, the way Francis said he was; if you don't, stay near it in your mind, breathing, without riding off.
Leprosy. The illness that young Francis of Assisi feared, until he got down from his horse and kissed the hand of a man who had it, and what was bitter turned sweet.
Your line: what was bitter became sweet. In his telling, the Lord did the leading. See you tomorrow.

815.title: Francis and the Sultan (1219)
815.hook: in the middle of a crusade, Francis crosses the lines to meet Sultan al-Kamil, and is received with courtesy
815.howItsDone: Franciscans and other Christians sometimes recall this meeting at interfaith gatherings with Muslims, and some Franciscan communities live and work in Muslim-majority countries.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Francis on the road, leprosy, and your line, what was bitter became sweet.

A crusader army is camped outside Damietta, in Egypt, and the war is going on all around it. Into the camp comes a barefoot friar from Assisi, with a companion, Brother Illuminato. He asks to cross over to the other side. In the later telling, he's warned he's walking to his death. He goes anyway. Out between the armies, he's seized by the Sultan's soldiers. Instead of being killed, he's brought before the Sultan himself, al-Malik al-Kamil, ruler of Egypt. An enemy preacher, in the middle of a war, standing before the man he's at war with.

The earliest witness is a bishop in the crusader camp, Jacques de Vitry, who wrote about it in a letter soon after. In paraphrase: Francis went to the Sultan and preached to him for some days, and the Sultan listened to him closely. Then the Sultan had him escorted back to the camp safely, with respect, and asked him to pray for him. That's the core. Later biographers add more. Bonaventure tells that Francis offered to walk through fire to show the truth of his faith, that the Sultan declined, and that he offered Francis gifts, which Francis refused. Stories grow. But the oldest letter is enough: a friar crossed the lines, spoke of his faith, and was received with courtesy and sent home alive. Notice both sides of that meeting. Francis went without a sword. And a Muslim ruler, in the middle of a war, listened to an enemy's preacher and protected him. Afterward, Francis wrote guidance for friars who wanted to live among Muslims. In paraphrase: they should not start arguments or disputes, but be subject to every human creature for God's sake, and say plainly that they are Christians; and only when they see that it pleases God, preach. Presence before persuasion. It echoes what Jesus told his followers when he sent them out, in the King James words: "into whatsoever house ye enter, first say, Peace be to this house." First, peace. Today some Christians and Muslims tell this story together, as a meeting that went better than the war around it.
screen: `FIRST SAY, PEACE BE TO THIS HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone on the other side of a line from you, in politics, faith, a family quarrel or a rival team, and picture crossing over the way Francis did: not to win, just to be there. What would courtesy look like with them: hearing them out to the end, a real greeting, a kind word about something they love? If you pray, pray for them by name; if you don't, wish them well, silently, by name.
Al-Kamil. The Muslim Sultan who received the unarmed friar Francis of Assisi with courtesy, and sent him back safe.
Your line: crossing the lines. That day, courtesy went both ways. Day eight hundred fifteen.

816.title: The first nativity scene
816.hook: at Greccio, Francis sets up a manger with a real ox and donkey
816.howItsDone: Churches and Christian homes often set out a nativity scene, or crib, during Advent and Christmas; some places hold living nativities with people and animals, and some families add the figure of the baby only on Christmas Eve.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Francis and the Sultan al-Kamil, and your line, crossing the lines.

Christmas night, in a small hill town called Greccio, in Italy. Men and women from the area are climbing toward a spot near the woods, carrying candles and torches that light up the dark. Friars have come in from other places. Waiting for them is a manger, filled with hay. Beside it stand an ox and a donkey, real ones, breathing in the cold. And next to the manger stands Francis of Assisi, singing the Gospel in a clear voice.

Thomas of Celano, Francis's early biographer, tells why. Francis asked a man of Greccio named John to help him prepare it, because, in paraphrase, he wanted to see with his own bodily eyes the hardship the baby went through: how he was laid in a manger, how he lay on hay with an ox and a donkey standing by. Not a painting. Not an idea. A real manger. Look at the Gospel's own words. Luke, in the King James Version: "she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn." A manger is a feeding trough. And notice: Luke never mentions an ox or a donkey. They come from a line in Isaiah that Christian tradition set beside the birth story: "The ox knoweth his owner, and the ass his master's crib." At Greccio the two texts stood side by side, in hay and breath. Then, Celano says, Mass was celebrated over the manger, and Francis preached about the child of Bethlehem, saying the name with great tenderness. A man there, Celano adds, saw in a vision a child lying still in the manger, and Francis bending to wake him. Celano reads that as a picture of the whole night: a child who'd been forgotten in many hearts, woken up again. Tradition calls Greccio the first nativity scene. Whatever came before it, the custom it's remembered for lives on, in cribs set out in churches and homes, some grand, some small enough to sit on a windowsill.
screen: `THE OX AND DONKEY COME FROM ISAIAH.`

segments.voice: If you have a nativity set, take out one piece and set it where you'll see it; if not, set down any small object on purpose, a cup, a stone, a folded cloth, as a place for something to arrive. If you pray, let it be a manger, an empty place made ready; if you don't, let it stand for something you want to make real, not just think about.
Nativity scene. What tradition calls the first one, at Greccio, where Francis set out a real manger, with hay, an ox and a donkey, so people could see the story with their own eyes.
Your line: a real manger. Hay, breath, and a story you can see. That's day eight hundred sixteen.

817.title: Welcome, sister death
817.hook: nearly blind and ill, Francis adds a verse for sister death to his song of the creatures, and dies singing
817.howItsDone: Franciscans and other Christians sing or pray Francis's Canticle of the Creatures, often called the Canticle of Brother Sun, and some read it at funerals or at the bedside of the dying.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Greccio, where Francis set out real hay, an ox and a donkey, and your line was a real manger.

Near the end of his life, Francis's eyes are failing and his body is worn out. And in that state, tradition says, he makes a song. It praises God for brother sun and sister moon, for brother wind and sister water, for brother fire, and for our sister, mother earth, who feeds us. The words are in the everyday Italian of his hills, not church Latin, plain enough to sing. Later, the story goes, he adds lines for people who forgive and bear trouble in peace. Then, when he learns he has little time left, he adds one more verse: praise for our sister, bodily death, whom no one living can escape.

His early biographer, Thomas of Celano, tells it this way. A doctor tells Francis that death is near, and Francis answers with one word first: welcome. Welcome, my sister death. Then he asks the brothers to sing his song to him, the new verse included. Celano says he asked to be laid on the bare ground and began a psalm, the one that opens, in the King James Bible, "I cried unto the LORD with my voice." He died, the story says, with that psalm in the room. Why sister? Because in this song everything is family: the sun a brother, the water a sister, the earth a mother. Death isn't let in from outside. She belongs to the household of creation. Francis isn't pretending death is pleasant; he is ill and in pain. He is naming it as kin. Behind that is Paul's faith: "O death, where is thy sting?" For Paul, Christ's rising has taken the sting out. And the song is honest. Right after the welcome, it warns those who die in grave sin and blesses those death finds doing God's will. Not every Christian speaks of death this gently. Christians also keep a long practice of grief and lament, and John's Gospel says that on the way to the tomb of his friend Lazarus, "Jesus wept." Both live in one church. Francis's word is one way of facing the end: open the door, use her name, and let the singing go on.

If a loss is close right now, skip this and simply breathe; that is a full practice too. Otherwise, notice the breath going in and out, a gift that won't go on forever, and say two words quietly, sister death. If you pray, borrow the psalm Francis began, I cried unto the LORD with my voice; if not, let the breath carry the minute.
Welcome. What Francis said, by Celano's account, when he heard death was near. He greeted her as a sister, not an enemy.
Your line: sister death. Not an enemy at the door, but family. See you tomorrow.

818.title: Clare
818.hook: Francis's friend who founded the Poor Clares and, tradition says, faced down soldiers holding the sacrament
818.howItsDone: The Poor Clares live an enclosed life of prayer in convents around the world, and Catholics and some Anglicans keep a feast day for Saint Clare.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Francis greeted death with one word, welcome, and your line was sister death.

Soldiers are coming over the wall of a small convent outside Assisi. Inside are women with no weapons, and their abbess is sick in bed. Here's what the old account says she does. She has herself carried to the door. She asks for the sacrament, the consecrated bread kept in a small box, to be set in front of her. She bows down before it and prays. And the soldiers, the story says, turn back and leave. The woman at the door is Clare, Francis's friend, whose sisters came to be called the Poor Clares.

Clare grew up in a noble family in Assisi, Francis's town. She heard him preach and wanted the life he lived: poor, simple, given to God. The Legend of Saint Clare says she slipped out of her family's house at night and went to Francis and his brothers, who cut her hair as a sign she was leaving the old life behind. When her relatives came to drag her home, she held onto the altar and showed them her shorn head, and they let her be. She settled at a little church called San Damiano, and other women came, her own sister among them. Their life was enclosed, prayerful and poor, and for years Clare asked church leaders to let her sisters own nothing at all. Back to the door. In some tellings, as she prays before the sacrament, a voice answers that God will always guard them. Whatever you make of it, the story says something about Clare: her defense was not a wall or a sword, but stillness and prayer before what she held most holy. Catholics and other Christians honor her as a saint. The same Legend tells of her last days. Lying ill, she speaks to her own soul: go forth in peace, for you will have a good escort. The woman who walked out of her father's house at night ends by sending her soul out the door, without fear.
screen: `OUT OF HER FATHER'S HOUSE AT NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Stand in a doorway, any door, feet on the floor and hands loose, and breathe. Think of what comes through doorways in your life, news, people, worry, and neither block it nor rush out to meet it. If you pray, hold in mind someone facing something frightening today; if not, let the breath slow and the doorframe hold you up.

819.title: Dominic's preachers
819.hook: a Spanish priest founds an order to preach, study and live poor
819.howItsDone: Dominican friars and sisters still pray together, study and preach, and lay people also join Dominican communities to share that life of prayer and learning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Clare met soldiers at San Damiano with prayer, and your line was go forth in peace.

A famine hits a Spanish town while a young student is there. Books then are handwritten on animal skin and very costly, and his are full of his own notes. His early biographer, Jordan of Saxony, says he sold them, notes and all, and gave the money to the hungry. His reason: he would not study on dead skins while people were starving. The student is Dominic. Years later he'll found a family of friars whose whole life is built on books and on giving away.

Dominic becomes a priest, and on a journey through southern France he meets a movement called the Cathars. Their teachers live strict, plain lives, and teach that the physical world is not God's good work. Jordan tells of one night at an inn. The innkeeper holds Cathar beliefs, and Dominic sits up with him all night, talking, listening, answering. By morning, Jordan says, the man returns to the church's faith. That night shows Dominic's method: not force, but conversation, patience, and a life as plain as anyone's. So he gathers men to live that way: travel on foot, own little, beg for bread, and preach. The church comes to call them the Order of Preachers; people call them Dominicans. And here's what stands out. Dominic wants his preachers to study, so he sends them to the towns where universities are growing. To preach well, they have to know well. Prayer and books together. A later Dominican, Thomas Aquinas, gave the idea words that stuck: to contemplate, and to hand on to others what you have contemplated. The history isn't all bright. A crusade was fought in the same region against the Cathars, and later Dominicans served in the Inquisition. Christians today still reckon with that. But Dominic's own picture was a man at an inn, awake all night, taking someone seriously enough to listen.

what it means: Dominic's preachers walked, owned little, studied hard, and talked with people as patiently as he did at the inn.

chat.says: Why did Dominic make his friars study so much? Isn't preaching mostly about passion?
options: To preach well they had to know well: take it in through prayer and study, then hand it on.
He wanted them to win debates, so for him study came to matter more than prayer did.
Study kept them settled in university towns, so they wouldn't have to travel or beg.
chat.meaning: Dominic sent his preachers to study so they could preach well. Aquinas put it as contemplating, then handing on what you contemplated.
